children: Titan’s Priya Mathilakath Pillai on redesigning work for AI, strengthening middle managers and building trust, adaptability and belonging across diverse workforces

As artificial intelligence reshapes jobs and organisations rethink how work gets done, the role of HR is moving beyond traditional people practices towards shaping workforce strategy, culture and capability. For organisations with diverse employee groups, the challenge is also to balance productivity and transformation with trust, belonging and long-term career growth.

Priya Mathilakath Pillai, Chief People Officer (Designate), Titan Company, discusses how organisations can redesign work for an AI-led future, strengthen the role of middle managers and build an employee experience that works across frontline, manufacturing and corporate teams. She also shares her perspective on DEIB, high-trust workplaces and why continuously renewing talent will be a defining people challenge for Indian businesses.

As AI and automation reshape roles across industries, how should organisations approach workforce redesign? What does a genuinely AI-ready workforce look like beyond simply training employees to use new tools?

I think we are asking the wrong question when we talk about AI readiness. Most organisations are focused on whether employees know how to use AI. The more strategic question is whether organisations are redesigning work itself.For decades, organisations were built on three assumptions: information was scarce, expertise was concentrated, and decisions moved up the hierarchy. AI is challenging all three. The real workforce redesign challenge is therefore not technology adoption. It is the redistribution of work, judgement and decision-making.

At Titan, whether we are talking about a craftsperson designing jewellery, a store associate building customer relationships, a manufacturing supervisor improving quality or a leader making strategic choices, the most valuable contribution increasingly lies in judgement, creativity, context and problem-solving.Technology can augment expertise. It cannot replace human context.

One aspect of workforce redesign that receives far less attention is the intergenerational workforce challenge. Many middle managers today are simultaneously leading employees whose expectations of work have been shaped by very different realities. In the same team, you may have employees who grew up valuing stability, hierarchy and expertise alongside employees who value flexibility, experimentation and rapid progression.

AI is accelerating that complexity. Managers are not simply helping people adopt new technology. They are helping different generations interpret what that technology means for their careers, their identity and their future relevance.Organisations need to shape the transition, not resist the technology. That means reskilling people, redesigning jobs, anticipating displaced capabilities and establishing responsible AI principles before disruption forces those conversations.

The organisations that outperform will not necessarily be those deploying AI the most. They will be those that redesign work fastest while helping people adapt with confidence. And that requires leaders to be comfortable saying, 'We are learning too.' In periods of transformation, vulnerability is not a weakness. It is often what creates the trust required for people to adapt.

Middle managers are increasingly under pressure to manage hybrid teams, changing employee expectations and AI-driven transformation. Why has the middle-management layer become so critical, and how should organisations rethink its role?

I often say strategy does not fail in the boardroom. It fails in translation.And middle managers are responsible for that translation.Most employees experience the organisation through their manager, not through the CEO, business leader or CHRO. Managers interpret change, drive performance, build engagement, shape culture and increasingly help people navigate ambiguity.

Today's managers are expected to improve productivity, integrate AI, develop talent, manage well-being and create engagement, all while delivering business outcomes. That is a much broader mandate than middle management carried out even five years ago. Which is why I believe we need to stop viewing managers as supervisors and start viewing them as organisational multipliers.

Their job is not simply to manage work. Their job is to increase the capacity of teams to perform, adapt and grow. At Titan, we increasingly see managerial effectiveness not only through results delivered but through future capability created.How many future leaders did they develop? How much adaptability did they create? How many people became more capable because they worked with them?In an environment characterised by continuous change, managerial capability could become one of the most important competitive differentiators an organisation has.

Retail and manufacturing have large frontline workforces, while corporate teams operate in very different environments. How can organisations create a consistent employee experience and culture across diverse workforce segments?

The challenge is not creating one employee experience. The challenge is creating one sense of belonging.A manufacturing employee in Hosur, a retail associate serving customers and a corporate employee sitting at headquarters operate in very different realities. Trying to make all their experiences identical is neither practical nor desirable.What should remain consistent is the employee promise.At Titan, we often think about our employee promise through a simple lens: Be. Build. Belong.Be reflects the freedom to bring your authentic self to work and be respected for who you are.

Build reflects the opportunity to create, contribute, learn and grow through meaningful work.Belong reflects our belief that every employee should feel connected to the organisation, its purpose and its people, regardless of role or location.What is important is that these three elements apply equally to a craftsperson in manufacturing, a retail associate serving customers and a corporate employee driving strategy.The experiences may look different. The opportunities may look different. The context may be different.
But every employee should be able to say: I can be myself here. I can build a fulfilling career here. I feel like I belong here.
That is how culture scales across a diverse organisation. Not through standardisation, but through a shared employee promise that is experienced consistently in different contexts.

Employee expectations around trust, flexibility, purpose and career growth have changed significantly. What are the biggest shifts you are seeing in the employer-employee relationship, and how should HR respond?

The relationship between employees and organisations has fundamentally matured. Employees are no longer looking for organisations to manage their careers. They are looking for organisations that help them build careers.People are seeking growth more than stability, development more than direction and authenticity more than promises. Increasingly, employees evaluate organisations almost the way consumers evaluate brands. They look for consistency between what an organisation says and what it actually does.

This changes HR's role significantly. The future of HR is not programme design. It is ecosystem design.But I think there is an even bigger question emerging for our profession. Is HR merely helping the business execute difficult choices? Or are we accountable for understanding and shaping the consequences of those choices? Historically, HR often focused on people impact assessments. Increasingly, I believe our role is evolving towards system impact stewardship.

Every major decision about automation, restructuring, workforce models, productivity or growth creates second- and third-order consequences across culture, capability and trust.HR's responsibility is not simply to assess those consequences after decisions are made. It is to help leaders understand them before decisions are made. HR should not become the conscience that simply says 'No'. Nor should HR become the business function that simply makes 'Yes' happen.The role is more complex than either of those extremes.
Modern HR leaders increasingly have to hold multiple tensions simultaneously:
Efficiency versus humanity
Shareholder value versus stakeholder value
Short-term survival versus long-term capability
Equality versus equity
Technology-led productivity versus human employability
Performance differentiation versus belonging
Business relevance versus independence of judgement
Speed of decision-making versus quality of consequence

And perhaps the most important paradox is this:The more strategic HR becomes, the greater the risk that HR loses the very human lens that makes the function distinctive.Our challenge is not choosing one side. It is helping organisations manage those tensions responsibly.

DEIB has moved from being largely a policy conversation to becoming part of organisational culture and business strategy. What does meaningful DEIB look like in practice, particularly across frontline, manufacturing and corporate environments?

For me, the real test of DEIB is not representation. It is participation.Representation tells us who is in the room. Participation tells us whose voice influences decisions.Across manufacturing, retail and corporate environments, the specific challenges may differ, but the principle remains the same.

Every individual should have equitable access to opportunity, visibility, growth and influence.Meaningful inclusion shows up in very practical ways. Who receives developmental opportunities? Who gets exposure? Whose ideas are heard? Who receives sponsorship? Who progresses into leadership roles?Titan views inclusion as a business capability rather than a compliance objective.

Diverse organisations make better decisions because they benefit from a broader range of perspectives.But that benefit only materialises when leaders create environments where those perspectives are actively sought and genuinely valued.Inclusion ultimately becomes less about policy and more about leadership behaviour.

With organisations increasingly focused on productivity and business outcomes, how can HR strike the right balance between performance expectations and building high-trust workplaces where employees feel empowered to perform?

I think one of the biggest misconceptions in organisations is that trust and performance sit on opposite ends of a spectrum.In reality, high-performing organisations are often high-trust organisations.When trust is low, organisations compensate with layers of controls, reviews and approvals.Decision-making slows. Energy gets consumed in managing processes rather than creating value.

Trust enables speed. And increasingly, speed is a competitive advantage.That said, trust should not be confused with comfort.High-trust organisations are not necessarily easy organisations. They are organisations where expectations are clear, feedback is candid and accountability is strong.

At Titan, we have always believed that performance and humanity reinforce each other rather than compete with each other.Leadership vulnerability plays a role here. Not because leaders need to have all the answers. But because authenticity creates credibility.People are far more willing to commit to ambitious goals when they trust the individuals leading them.
Looking ahead over the next 3–5 years, what do you believe will be the defining people challenge for Indian businesses, and what should CHROs and business leaders start doing now to prepare for it?

I do not believe the defining challenge will be attracting talent. I believe it will be continuously renewing talent.Historically, organisations built capabilities that remained relevant for years.Today, the shelf life of skills, business models and even leadership approaches is shrinking rapidly.The challenge for Indian businesses will be building organisations that can repeatedly reinvent themselves without losing their identity.

That is not simply a workforce planning issue. It is a culture issue. The organisations that succeed will be those that create adaptability at scale while maintaining belonging, trust and purpose. Looking ahead, I believe HR must increasingly become the function that helps organisations see around corners.Not just asking: 'Is this legal?' 'Can we afford it?' 'Will employees accept it?' But asking: What kind of organisation are we becoming as a consequence of this decision?

That is where strategy, culture and ethics intersect. And arguably that is where HR has a unique responsibility.We must shape the transition rather than resist it.We must establish responsible AI principles.We must redesign jobs before they become obsolete.We must bring a long-term capability lens to business decisions.

And we must be the ethical boundary-setter, ensuring decisions are based on legitimate business and capability criteria rather than convenience or vulnerability.For Titan in particular, this is ultimately about protecting our long-term trust premium while enabling the business to make the difficult choices required for growth.People cost is visible on a P&L. Capability, trust and culture rarely are.Yet those are often the assets that determine whether a business succeeds for a quarter or for a generation.
Mahek Asghar
BW Reporters The author is a trainee correspondent at BW Businessworld.
